quests.instruction: Which soft, wrinkly part, shaped a bit like a big walnut, is hidden inside your head?
quests.hint: A hard bony case protects it.
quests.explanation: The brain is the control center of your body. Its wrinkles give it more surface, so more thinking power fits inside your skull.
quests.funFact: Your brain has roughly 86 billion nerve cells.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body figures out that something hurts, yet has no pain sensors of its own?
quests.hint: It is the one that makes sense of all the messages.
quests.explanation: Pain messages travel along nerves to your brain, which decides that it hurts. The brain's own tissue has no pain sensors.
quests.funFact: Doctors can sometimes work on the brain while the patient is awake and chatting, because the brain tissue itself does not feel pain.

quests.instruction: Which hard, rounded case of bones protects your brain like a helmet?
quests.hint: You can feel it under your hair.
quests.explanation: The skull is a strong box of joined bones that surrounds and protects the brain.
quests.funFact: Your skull has 22 bones, and all of them are joined together except your lower jaw.

quests.instruction: Which muscle has two sides, one pumping blood to your lungs and the other pumping it to the rest of your body?
quests.hint: It is a muscle that never stops pumping.
quests.explanation: The right side of the heart sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen, and the left side sends it out to the body.
quests.funFact: The lub-dub sound of a heartbeat comes from little flaps inside the heart, called valves, snapping shut.

quests.instruction: Which liquid travels through your heart, brings food and oxygen to every part of you, and carries waste away?
quests.hint: You see it when you get a cut.
quests.explanation: Blood is the delivery truck of your body. It drops off oxygen and nutrients and picks up waste to be removed.
quests.funFact: Blood is red because red blood cells contain a protein with iron in it.

quests.instruction: Which stretchy tubes carry blood from your heart out to every part of you and back again?
quests.hint: You can see some as bluish lines under pale skin.
quests.explanation: Blood vessels branch into smaller and smaller tubes until they reach every part of your body.
quests.funFact: Laid end to end, the blood vessels of an adult could stretch around the Earth more than twice.

quests.instruction: Your left lung is a little smaller than your right lung. Which part does it make room for?
quests.hint: It sits slightly toward the left of your chest.
quests.explanation: The heart is tilted a bit to the left, so the left lung is a little smaller to make room for it.
quests.funFact: The right lung has three sections, called lobes, and the left lung has two.

quests.instruction: Which tube carries air from your throat down into your lungs?
quests.hint: You can feel its ridges at the front of your neck.
quests.explanation: Air goes in through your nose or mouth, down the windpipe, and into your lungs.
quests.funFact: The windpipe is held open by rings of tough, bendy cartilage.

quests.instruction: Your blood carries a waste gas called carbon dioxide to which parts, so you can breathe it out?
quests.hint: They sit in your chest, on both sides of your heart.
quests.explanation: In your lungs, blood drops off carbon dioxide and picks up fresh oxygen, a swap that happens with every breath.
quests.funFact: Plants do the opposite: they take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

quests.instruction: After you swallow, food lands in a stretchy, J-shaped bag that mixes it with strong juices. Which part is it?
quests.hint: It is under your ribs, mostly on the left.
quests.explanation: The stomach churns food with digestive juices and turns it into a thick soup.
quests.funFact: A stomach can stretch to hold about a liter of food and drink.

quests.instruction: What is the tube that carries swallowed food from your throat to your stomach?
quests.hint: It runs behind your windpipe.
quests.explanation: The food pipe connects your throat to your stomach, so everything you swallow travels through it.
quests.funFact: The food pipe is about 25 centimeters long in an adult.

quests.instruction: After the stomach, food moves into long, winding tubes where your body takes in the good parts. What are they called?
quests.hint: They are coiled up inside your tummy.
quests.explanation: The intestines pass nutrients from food into your blood, and the leftovers move on and leave your body.
quests.funFact: An adult's small intestine is about six meters long, longer than a car.

quests.instruction: Which curved bones form a cage around your heart and lungs?
quests.hint: You can feel them on your sides.
quests.explanation: Ribs curve around the chest like the bars of a cage, protecting the heart and lungs.
quests.funFact: The lowest two pairs of ribs are called floating ribs, because they do not attach to the breastbone in front.

quests.instruction: Which stack of small bones runs down your back and protects the bundle of nerves inside it?
quests.hint: You can feel its bumps down the middle of your back.
quests.explanation: The spine, or backbone, holds you upright and shields the spinal cord, the main road for messages between your brain and body.
quests.funFact: A grown-up's spine has 33 small bones, though the lowest ones are joined together.

quests.instruction: Which soft center inside many bones makes new blood cells?
quests.hint: It fills the hollow inside certain bones.
quests.explanation: Bone marrow is a soft, spongy tissue that builds red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.
quests.funFact: Your marrow makes millions of new red blood cells every second.

quests.instruction: Which dome-shaped muscle under your lungs flattens and moves down when you breathe in?
quests.hint: It is a sheet of muscle between your chest and your tummy.
quests.explanation: When the diaphragm moves down, your chest gets roomier and air rushes into your lungs.
quests.funFact: A hiccup is a sudden twitch of the diaphragm.

quests.instruction: When you flex to show off a strong arm, the bulge on the front of your upper arm is which muscle?
quests.hint: It helps bend your elbow.
quests.explanation: The biceps tightens and gets shorter, which pulls your forearm up and bends your elbow.
quests.funFact: The name biceps means two heads in Latin, because the muscle has two parts that join into one tendon.

quests.instruction: Which parts in the walls of your stomach and intestines squeeze in waves to push food along without you having to think about it?
quests.hint: The same kind of parts help you move your arms and legs.
quests.explanation: These muscles work on their own, so digestion goes on while you play, learn, or sleep.
quests.funFact: Your gut has so many nerves that it is sometimes called a second brain.

quests.instruction: Which part of your body holds the roots of your hair, the glands that make sweat, and covers you from head to toe?
quests.hint: It is the biggest organ you can see.
quests.explanation: Skin holds the tiny roots that grow your hair and the glands that make sweat.
quests.funFact: Your skin grows along with you, getting bigger as your body grows.

quests.instruction: Which natural coloring in your skin, hair, and eyes helps shield your skin from the sun?
quests.hint: People have different amounts of it, which is why skin comes in so many shades.
quests.explanation: Melanin gives skin its color and absorbs some of the sun's harmful rays. Everyone still needs sun protection.
quests.funFact: Time in the sun makes your skin produce more melanin, and that is what a tan is.

quests.instruction: When a deep cut heals, it can leave a mark of tough new tissue. What is it called?
quests.hint: It is often a pale or shiny line where the skin healed.
quests.explanation: A scar forms when the body repairs deeper damage with tough, tightly packed fibers. It is a sign of healing.
quests.funFact: Scars do not have sweat glands or hair roots.

quests.instruction: Which two bean-shaped parts clean your blood and make pee?
quests.hint: They sit toward the back of your body, just under your ribs.
quests.explanation: Kidneys filter waste and extra water out of your blood and send them out of your body as pee.
quests.funFact: Your kidneys filter all of your blood many times every day.

quests.instruction: Which bundle of nerves runs inside your spine, carrying messages between your brain and your body?
quests.hint: It is protected by the bones of your back.
quests.explanation: The spinal cord is the main road for messages. Signals from your body travel up it to the brain, and orders travel back down.
quests.funFact: Your spinal cord is about as thick as your finger.

quests.instruction: Which tough bands hold the bones together at a joint?
quests.hint: They connect one bone to another bone.
quests.explanation: Ligaments are strong, slightly stretchy bands that keep the bones in a joint from slipping apart. Tendons are different: they join muscle to bone.
quests.funFact: Stretching too far can strain a ligament, which is why warming up helps.

quests.instruction: Which tiny cells in your blood fight germs?
quests.hint: They are part of your body's defense team.
quests.explanation: White blood cells find and attack germs that get inside your body.
quests.funFact: Your body makes more white blood cells when it is fighting an infection.

quests.instruction: When you get a small cut, tiny pieces in your blood stick together to plug it. What are they called?
quests.hint: They help a scab form.
quests.explanation: Platelets rush to a cut and clump together, which helps stop the bleeding and starts a scab.
quests.funFact: Platelets live only about a week to ten days, so your marrow keeps making new ones.

quests.instruction: Two small lumps at the back of your throat help catch germs that enter through your mouth. What are they?
quests.hint: You can see them when you open wide and say ahh.
quests.explanation: Tonsils are part of your body's germ-fighting team, standing guard at the back of the throat.
quests.funFact: Some people have their tonsils removed if they get sore throats very often, and they stay healthy without them.

quests.instruction: If your heart is like a pump, which part is like a pair of bellows that pulls air in and pushes it out?
quests.hint: They get bigger when you breathe in.
quests.explanation: Lungs expand to take in air and shrink to push it out, a bit like the bellows people use to fan a fire.
quests.funFact: A baby's lungs take their first breath within seconds of being born.

quests.instruction: Strong juices in your stomach break down food. Which part's lining makes slimy mucus to protect itself from those juices?
quests.hint: It is the stretchy bag that food lands in after you swallow.
quests.explanation: The stomach wall is coated with mucus that shields it from its own digestive juices.
quests.funFact: The lining of your stomach replaces itself every few days.

quests.instruction: All of your bones together make up what?
quests.hint: It gives your body its shape.
quests.explanation: Your skeleton is the frame of your body, a bit like the frame of a house.
quests.funFact: Your skeleton weighs only about 15 percent of your total body weight.
